title: Reported speech
blurb: Report what someone said or asked — říkal, že..., ptal se, jestli... — without English-style tense backshifting.

vocab.example: Zeptal se mě, jestli mám čas.

grammarNote.title: No tense backshift — and jestli for yes/no questions
grammarNote.text: Unlike English, Czech reported speech does not shift the tense back. If the original statement was in the present tense, it stays present when reported: direct „Jsem unavený“ becomes „Řekl, že je unavený“ — not „byl unavený“. English speakers instinctively want to backshift ("he said he was tired"), but Czech simply repeats the original statement's tense from the original speaker's viewpoint. For reported yes/no questions, use jestli (or the more formal zda) where English uses "whether/if": Ptá se, jestli přijdeš. For reported wh-questions, keep the original question word and normal statement word order — no inversion: Zeptal se, kdy přijedeš. Finally, prý is a handy indeclinable particle meaning "apparently / so they say" that lets you report something secondhand without building a full „že“ clause: Prý je nemocný.

check.prompt: Direct speech: „Jsem unavený.“ How is this correctly reported in Czech?
check.explanation: Czech doesn't backshift tense — the original present tense „jsem“ stays present as „je“ in the reported version.
check.note: English backshifts ("he said he was tired"); Czech does not. This is the single most common reported-speech mistake for English speakers.

check.prompt: „Zeptal se, jestli mám čas“ uses jestli because it reports a yes/no question.
check.explanation: Yes/no questions are reported with jestli (or the more formal zda), the Czech equivalent of "whether".
check.note: Wh-questions work differently — they keep their own question word (kdy, kde, co…) instead of switching to jestli.

check.prompt: Přímá řeč: „Mám hlad.“ Nepřímá řeč: Řekla, že ___ hlad.
check.explanation: The present tense „mám“ stays present in reported speech — only the person changes, to „má“.

check.prompt: Přímá řeč: „Kdy přijedeš?“ (ptala se) → Nepřímá řeč: Zeptala se, ___ přijedu.
check.explanation: Wh-question words are kept unchanged when reporting a question; only the pronoun/verb person shifts.

title: Connecting ideas
blurb: Link clauses like a fluent speaker — cause, consequence, and concession beyond a basic a/ale.

vocab.example: Ačkoli je mladý, hodně toho ví.
Bylo mu špatně. I přesto šel do práce.

vocab.translation: on one hand… on the other…
vocab.example: Jednak nemám čas, jednak nemám peníze.

grammarNote.title: Cause vs. consequence vs. concession — picking the right connector
grammarNote.text: These connectors fall into three families, and mixing them up is the most common B1 mistake. Cause: protože ("because") introduces the reason and answers "why" — Nejdu ven, protože prší. Consequence: takže and proto both mean "so/therefore" and introduce the result, not the reason — takže is the everyday spoken choice and often starts a new clause after a comma (Prší, takže nejdu ven), while proto is slightly more formal and commonly paired with "a" (Bylo pozdě, a proto jsme odešli). Concession: i když, přestože, and ačkoli all mean "even though/although" and introduce a clause that contrasts with the expected outcome — i když is the everyday spoken choice, přestože and ačkoli are more formal/written, and all three can open the sentence (Přestože pršelo, šel ven). Unlike German, none of these connectors force the verb into a special "second position" — Czech word order after them stays as flexible as in any other clause.

check.prompt: Nestihl jsem autobus, ___ jsem přišel pozdě.
check.explanation: Takže introduces the consequence/result — "jsem přišel pozdě" is the result of missing the bus, not the reason for it.
check.note: Protože would go the other way: „Přišel jsem pozdě, protože jsem nestihl autobus.“

check.prompt: Přestože and i když both introduce a concession clause and are roughly interchangeable, with přestože sounding more formal.
check.explanation: Correct — both mean "even though"; i když is the everyday spoken version, přestože leans more formal/written.
check.note: Ačkoli sits at the most formal/literary end of this same group.

check.prompt: ___ je mu osmdesát, pořád běhá maraton.
check.explanation: Any of the concession connectors (i když, přestože, ačkoli) fits here — the clause contrasts age with an unexpectedly active habit.

check.prompt: Combine with proto: „Prší. Nejdu ven.“ → „Prší, ___ nejdu ven.“
check.explanation: Proto links the cause (prší) to its consequence (nejdu ven), usually introduced with „a proto“ in running speech.

title: Idiomatic & phrasal expressions
blurb: Common fixed Czech phrases that don't translate word-for-word — recognize them and start using them naturally.

vocab.translation: to know something inside out (lit. have it in one's pinky)
to rack one's brain over it (lit. break one's head)
to have a guilty conscience (lit. have butter on one's head)
vocab.example: Mluví o tom málo, asi má máslo na hlavě.

vocab.translation: to beat around the bush (lit. walk around hot porridge)
vocab.example: Nechoď kolem horké kaše a řekni to rovnou.

vocab.translation: what a relief (lit. a stone fell from my heart)
vocab.example: Když jsem to uslyšel, spadl mi kámen ze srdce.

vocab.translation: it's all Greek to me (lit. it's a Spanish village to me)
vocab.example: Ta smlouva je mi španělská vesnice.

vocab.translation: to be in the clear / well set up (lit. be beyond the water)
vocab.example: Když to podepíšeme, jsme za vodou.

vocab.translation: to be a bit odd/crazy (lit. have one gear more)
vocab.example: Občas mám pocit, že má o kolečko víc.

grammarNote.title: Idioms don't translate — but they still inflect
grammarNote.text: An idiom's meaning belongs to the whole phrase, not to its individual words, so translating word-by-word almost always fails — lámat si hlavu doesn't mean "to break your head", it means "to rack your brain / worry about something". What doesn't disappear, though, is normal grammar: the verb inside the idiom still conjugates and the fixed noun/case combination stays put around it, e.g. mít v malíčku conjugates exactly like any other mít sentence (mám to v malíčku, máš to v malíčku, má to v malíčku…), while „v malíčku“ itself never changes. A good way to learn these is to lean on the literal image as a memory hook even though it isn't the real meaning — a stone falling off your heart (spadl mi kámen ze srdce) is a vivid enough picture to remember "relief" by. One more thing worth knowing: register varies — most of these are perfectly normal in everyday conversation, but a few (like mít máslo na hlavě) feel casual and wouldn't belong in formal writing.

check.prompt: „Nelámej si s tím hlavu“ means roughly:
check.explanation: Literally "don't break your head over it", but idiomatically it means "don't worry / don't stress about it".
check.note: The verb lámat (to break) is doing real conjugation work here — já si lámu hlavu, ty si lámeš hlavu, etc. all follow the same pattern.

check.prompt: „To je mi španělská vesnice“ is used when something makes perfect sense to you.
check.explanation: The opposite — it means something is completely incomprehensible to you, equivalent to "it's all Greek to me".
check.note: This is one of many European languages that names a specific place instead of "Greek" — always worth double-checking, never assume from your own language.

check.prompt: Když jsem uslyšel dobrou zprávu, spadl mi kámen ___ srdce.
check.explanation: This idiom is fixed with the preposition ze (from): spadl mi kámen ze srdce.

check.prompt: „On má máslo na hlavě.“ → Rewrite for „já“: Já ___ máslo na hlavě.
check.explanation: Only the verb mít conjugates across persons (mám, máš, má…) — the rest of the idiom, máslo na hlavě, never changes.
